sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) is a B-cell maturation antigen-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy approved in the USA for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) as early as following first relapse, based on pivotal CARTITUDE-1 (≥ 4 prior lines of therapy [LOT]) and CARTITUDE-4 (1–3 prior LOT) trials, which reported high response rates and prolonged survival. In CARTITUDE-1 and CARTITUDE-4, rates of all-grade parkinsonism were 6% and < 1%, respectively, while rates of cranial nerve palsy were 3% and 9%, respectively. This study aimed to characterize new-onset nonimmune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (non-ICANS) neurologic events (NEs) among patients with RRMM receiving cilta-cel after 1–3 or ≥ 4 prior LOT.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This retrospective study used two real-world data sources: open and closed insurance claims from the Komodo Research Database (February 2021–November 2024), and electronic medical records from Loopback Analytics (February 2021–December 2024). New-onset non-ICANS NEs, including parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsy, and Guillain–Barré syndrome, were assessed from cilta-cel infusion until the end of clinical activity, death, or end of data availability. Analyses were conducted separately by database and stratified by LOT.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In patients with 1–3 prior LOT (Komodo: 124; Loopback: 79), over a median follow-up of 3.4–3.5 months, cranial nerve palsy occurred in 5.6% and 5.1% in Komodo and Loopback, respectively, with no parkinsonism or Guillain–Barré syndrome observed. In patients with ≥ 4 prior LOT (Komodo: 524; Loopback: 191), over a median follow-up of 13.2–13.3 months, parkinsonism occurred in 1.0% in both databases, cranial nerve palsy in 4.6% and 1.0%, and Guillain–Barré syndrome in 0.2% and 0.5% in Komodo and Loopback, respectively.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this real-world study, rates of non-ICANS NEs post-cilta-cel infusion across two databases were comparable to or lower than prior trials or real-world studies, reinforcing the favorable risk–benefit profile of cilta-cel in routine practice.

tr.td: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) is a chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy that has demonstrated high, sustained response and prolonged survival in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM).

In the pivotal CARTITUDE-1 (≥ 4 prior lines of therapy [LOT]) and CARTITUDE-4 (1–3 prior LOT) trials, nonimmune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (non-ICANS) neurologic events (NEs) were reported, but these events need to be better characterized in routine care.

This retrospective study aimed to describe new-onset non-ICANS NEs among patients with RRMM receiving cilta-cel after 1–3 or ≥ 4 prior LOT, using two real-world data sources (Komodo Research Database and Loopback Analytics).

bold.italic: What was learned from the study?

tr.td: In this real-world study of patients treated with 1–3 prior LOT (Komodo: 124; Loopback: 79) and ≥ 4 prior LOT (Komodo: 524; Loopback: 191), rates of new-onset non-ICANS NEs, including parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsy, and Guillain–Barré syndrome, were comparable to or lower than prior trials or real-world studies.
These results reinforce the favorable risk–benefit profile of cilta-cel for patients with RRMM in routine practice.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as a transformative therapeutic advancement for patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) [1]. Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) is a B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CAR-T therapy designed to induce targeted T-cell activation and proliferation [2, 3]. In February 2022, cilta-cel was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adults with RRMM after ≥ 4 prior lines of therapy (LOT) on the basis of results from the phase Ib/II CARTITUDE-1 trial, which demonstrated durable responses in heavily pretreated patients [4, 5]. Results from the phase 3 CARTITUDE-4 trial subsequently showed improved outcomes with cilta-cel in earlier lines, supporting the expansion of the FDA indication in April 2024 to patients with lenalidomide-refractory RRMM with ≥ 1 prior LOT [3, 6].

Across pivotal clinical trials, cilta-cel has demonstrated a favorable risk–benefit profile [3, 5]. As with other CAR-T therapies, adverse events have included cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), which were largely low grade and occurred within a predictable post-infusion window [3, 5, 7]. While neurologic toxicity following CAR-T therapy has historically been discussed in the context of ICANS, other non-ICANS neurologic events (NEs) have also been reported [7–9]. In clinical trials or case reports related to cilta-cel, non-ICANS NEs, including parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsy, and Guillain–Barré syndrome, have been reported, with variable incidence and limited description of timing and presentation [3, 5, 10]. Emerging real-world studies have described non-ICANS NEs following cilta-cel in clinical practice; however, there are limited clinical details. There is a need to better characterize the incidence, timing, presentation, and management of non-ICANS NEs in routine care [9, 11, 12].

Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the rates and time-to-onset of new-onset non-ICANS NEs among patients with RRMM treated with commercial cilta-cel after 1–3 prior LOT and after ≥ 4 prior LOT using two large US real-world databases.

sec.title: Data Source
sec.p: We used two real-world data sources: open and closed insurance claims from the Komodo Research Database (February 2021–November 2024) and the Loopback Analytics database (February 2021–December 2024). Komodo is a claims-based database that captures more than 330 million patient journeys from over 150 payers, including commercial, Medicaid, and Medicare insurers. Loopback Analytics is an electronic medical records (EMR) database, including community and academic institutions in the USA. To our knowledge, the data captured patients with commercial use of cilta-cel (CARVYKTI®) in routine care, with dose, timing, and route of administration consistent with FDA-required labeling [13]. The authors obtained permission from Komodo and from Loopback Analytics to access and use the databases under license for this study. The study was considered exempt research under 45 CFR § 46.104(d)(4) as it involved only the secondary use of data that were de-identified in compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, specifically, 45 CFR § 164.514.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This was a retrospective longitudinal study of patients with RRMM treated with commercial cilta-cel. We defined the index date as the date of cilta-cel infusion on or after 28 February 2022 (date of initial cilta-cel FDA approval). The baseline period covered the 12 months prior to the infusion date, and the follow-up period extended from the infusion date to end of clinical activity, death, or end of data availability. Clinical activity spanned the time between the patients’ first and last claims or health records in the databases.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: The study included adult patients (i.e., ≥ 18 years) with multiple myeloma (≥ 2 diagnoses on separate dates, including ≥ 1 prior to cilta-cel infusion; see Table S1 for list of codes) who received cilta-cel after 1–3 or ≥ 4 prior LOT and had ≥ 12 months of clinical activity prior to infusion. To address potential left-censoring (resulting in potentially not observing all previous LOT), we considered all patients who received cilta-cel before 5 April 2024 (date of FDA approval in earlier lines) to have ≥ 4 prior LOT, after which patients with 1–3 and ≥ 4 prior LOT were classified on the basis of the number of LOT observed. Thus, cilta-cel administration in patients with 1–3 and ≥ 4 prior LOT aligned with the CARTITUDE-4 and CARTITUDE-1 patient populations, respectively.

We excluded patients with evidence of CAR-T therapy or a diagnosis of amyloidosis prior to infusion, without evidence of lymphodepleting chemotherapy, or with participation in a clinical trial during the cilta-cel LOT (Fig. 1).Fig. 1

sec.title: Study Outcomes and Statistical Analysis
sec.p: We defined new-onset non-ICANS NEs, including parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsy, and Guillain–Barré syndrome, as ≥ 2 diagnoses in any position (i.e., primary or secondary diagnosis) for the same condition on separate days within 30 days of each other, with no evidence of preexisting NEs during the baseline period (see Table S2 for list of codes). We used descriptive statistics to summarize baseline demographic and clinical characteristics. Sex and race were recorded in the two databases on the basis of self-reporting. In addition, we assessed the Quan-Charlson Comorbidity Index (Quan-CCI; a validated score that predicts a patient’s 10-year mortality risk and resource utilization on the basis of a list of comorbidities, weighted by severity) [14], calcium elevation, renal insufficiency, anemia, and bone lesions (i.e., CRAB symptoms), as well as frailty index score (a score ranging 0–1 based on a list of 31 comorbidities categorized in the following domains: morbidity, function, sensory loss, cognition and mood, and other; see Tables S3–S5) [15], as well as rates and time-to-onset of non-ICANS NEs.

sec.title: Baseline Characteristics
sec.p:
A total of 648 patients in Komodo (1–3 prior LOT: 124; ≥ 4 prior LOT: 524) and 270 patients in Loopback (1–3 prior LOT: 79; ≥ 4 prior LOT: 191) meeting eligibility criteria were included. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1. In patients with 1–3 prior LOT and ≥ 4 prior LOT, characteristics were largely similar in the Komodo and Loopback databases, other than the mean Quan-CCI score and the proportion of patients with mild-to-severe frailty, which may reflect differences in patient populations or inherent differences in the availability of comorbidity information between the two databases. sec.title: New-Onset Non-ICANS NEs
sec.p:
In patients with 1–3 prior LOT, over a median (interquartile range) follow-up of 3.4 (1.6–4.8) months in Komodo and 3.5 (1.8–5.8) months in Loopback, no cases of parkinsonism or Guillain–Barré syndrome were observed. In patients with ≥ 4 prior LOT, over a median (interquartile range) follow-up of 13.3 (7.2–19.5) months in Komodo and 13.2 (9.4–20.1) months in Loopback, parkinsonism occurred in five (1.0%) and two (1.0%) patients with a median time-to-onset of 36.0 days and 47.0 days, respectively. Cranial nerve palsy was observed in 24 (4.6%) patients in Komodo and 2 (1.0%) patients in Loopback within a median time-to-onset of 27.0 days and 35.5 days, respectively. Guillain–Barré syndrome occurred in one patient in both Komodo (0.2%) and Loopback (0.5%) with a time-to-onset of 47.0 days and 118.0 days, respectively (Table 2; Fig. 2B).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this real-world study using an administrative claims and an EMR database, the rates of new-onset non-ICANS NEs, including parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsy, and Guillain–Barré syndrome, were comparable to or lower than those reported in pivotal trials and previous real-world studies, with most events occurring within the first two months post-infusion [3, 5, 9, 12]. Findings were consistent in patients treated with cilta-cel in earlier and later LOT, and between the two databases, representing a diverse population of patients with different types of insurance and who were treated across various settings.

In the CARTITUDE-4 clinical trial (1–3 prior LOT), the incidence of parkinsonism was < 1% versus 6% in the CARTITUDE-1 clinical trial (≥ 4 prior LOT) [13]. In CARTITUDE-4, the incidence of cranial nerve palsy was 9% versus 3% in CARTITUDE-1 [13]. No cases of Guillain–Barré syndrome were reported in either trial. While results in our study were largely comparable, the lower rates observed in our study for parkinsonism compared with CARTITUDE-4 and CARTITUDE-1 may reflect differences in event ascertainment between clinical trial and routine care settings. Clinical trials involve close protocol-driven monitoring, which may lead to the identification of milder or transient events that are less likely to be recorded in claims or EMR data. These data sources are collected for billing and clinical purposes, rather than for research, and lack standardized protocol-based adverse event monitoring and reporting [16]. Thus, this study may have primarily captured clinically evident parkinsonism, potentially resulting in underreporting of less severe events. Indeed, rates of non-ICANS NEs reported in a real-world multicenter retrospective study by Sidana et al. were comparable to those observed in our study [9]. Among 236 patients who received cilta-cel in 2022 across 16 academic medical centers, reported rates of parkinsonism and cranial nerve palsy were 2% and 5%, respectively, over a median follow-up of 13 months [9]. A more recent real-world study, conducted by Lim et al., among 235 patients receiving commercial cilta-cel between 2022 and 2024 across three campuses of a large US academic medical center reported rates of 3.8% (parkinsonism) and 6.4% (cranial nerve palsy) over a median follow-up of 12 months [12].

The mechanisms underlying non-ICANS NEs following CAR-T therapy are not well understood. However, emerging evidence suggests that persistent expansion of CAR-positive (CAR+) T cells may contribute to non-ICANS NEs following CAR-T infusion, suggesting that prolonged immune activation may underlie these events [17, 18]. In addition, BCMA expression has been identified in the caudate nucleus and may be upregulated in inflammatory settings [18]. The caudate nucleus is part of the basal ganglia and involved in motor control [19]. It is hypothesized that parkinsonism may be an on-target, off-tumor effect of BCMA-targeting CAR-T therapies [18]. Further research is needed to establish the pathophysiologic mechanism of parkinsonism. Furthermore, in the CARTITUDE-4 trial, parkinsonism was not reported in patients who achieved at least a partial response or greater during bridging therapy [20]. While this suggests that effective disease control during bridging therapy may reduce the risk of parkinsonism, such relationships could not be evaluated in the current study owing to the low incidence of parkinsonism and limited clinical information in structured data. Taken together, these findings suggest that non-ICANS NEs may be due to late immune effects, rather than the acute mechanisms associated with ICANS. The low rates observed in this study reinforce the favorable risk–benefit profile of cilta-cel in the real world. These findings also underscore the importance of clinician awareness and symptom monitoring for NEs beyond the acute period when ICANS is typically observed to facilitate timely identification and appropriate management of these NEs.

The current study leveraged the broad population coverage of claims data and more clinical information available in EMR data, and the consistency of results across two large nationally representative databases supports the robustness of the observed estimates. However, some limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. Komodo is a claims database capturing diagnosis codes used for billing medical services, while Loopback is an EMR database that captures clinically relevant events recorded during patient follow-up visits. For both databases, care received outside of the network may not be fully captured, which may lead to missed diagnoses. In Loopback, out-of-network care may have led to an underestimation of comorbidities and rates of events. In addition, as with all retrospective analyses using real-world databases, the identification of non-ICANS NEs relied on diagnosis codes, which may be subject to misclassification, coding inaccuracies, or variability in the recording of events. The use of stringent criteria for identifying non-ICANS NEs (i.e., ≥ 2 diagnoses on separate days within 30 days) helps improve specificity and mitigates the identification of false-positive events, but reduces sensitivity, which may lead to underreporting of less severe events. Differences in center-specific coding practices may also partially explain discrepancies in event rates observed in claims versus EMR data; nonetheless, event rates observed were largely consistent between Komodo and Loopback, with the rates of cranial nerve palsy among patients with ≥ 4 prior LOT being the main difference observed between the two databases. Finally, the rates of new-onset non-ICANS NEs following cilta-cel should be interpreted in light of the duration of follow-up available, particularly in earlier LOT where events with longer time-to-onset may not have emerged yet. Nevertheless, as results showed among patients with ≥ 4 prior LOT, the majority of events occurred between 1 and 3 months post-infusion. As such, most events are expected to be captured within the current median follow-up duration of 3.4–3.5 months among patients with 1–3 prior LOT. Moreover, the low rates of events in this study precluded robust sex- or race-stratified analyses. Future real-world studies with longer follow-up are warranted to better characterize non-ICANS NEs, and their management and resolution as well as according to key demographic and clinical characteristics.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study using two large real-world databases, the rates of new-onset non-ICANS NEs following cilta-cel were comparable to or lower than pivotal trials and other real-world studies. This further expands on existing evidence of the favorable risk–benefit profile of cilta-cel in routine clinical practice. Continued investigation is warranted to identify potential predictive factors and to inform optimal monitoring strategies in patients receiving CAR-T therapy.
